## Learning Objectives

After completing this tutorial, you will be able to:

- Explain why a finite element evolution is $M\dot{\vc{u}} = \vc{F}$ rather
  than $\dot{\vc{u}} = \vc{F}$, and what $M$ collects
- Locate $M^{T}$ in the transient adjoint recursion, and say which block it
  sits in
- Derive the reduced interior evolution by partitioning $M$, and read off
  the $M_{id}\dot{\vc{g}}$ term that a time-varying boundary contributes
- Say which time steppers supply that term automatically and which need it
  analytically
- Measure the temporal convergence of a quantity of interest **and** of its
  gradient, and explain why they share an order


## The One Thing That Changes

[The steady tutorial](adjoint_steady_pde_concept.qmd) solved
$\vc{R}(\vc{u}, \vc{p}) = \vc{0}$ once and took one transposed solve. This
tutorial runs the same physics forward in time. Almost nothing about the
adjoint recipe changes --- it is still solve forward, solve backward,
assemble --- and this tutorial does not repeat it.

What changes is that a finite element evolution is not
$\dot{\vc{u}} = \vc{F}(\vc{u}, t)$. It is

$$
M \dot{\vc{u}} = \vc{F}(\vc{u}, t) ,
$$ {#eq-mass-ode}

where $M$ is the **mass matrix**, $M_{ij} = \int_\Omega \phi_i \phi_j$. It
is not the identity, it is not diagonal, and it does not go away. Wherever
it appears going forward, $M^{T}$ appears coming back.

Everything in this tutorial is a consequence of that one fact.


## A Reminder of What $M$ Is

[Evolving a PDE in time](galerkin_transient_usage.qmd) derives $M$ from the
weak form and explains why it is the Gram matrix of the basis rather than
the identity. That derivation is not repeated here. Three facts from it are
what the rest of this tutorial leans on:

- $M_{ij} = \int_\Omega \phi_i \phi_j$, so $M_{ij} \neq 0$ exactly when the
  basis functions at nodes $i$ and $j$ overlap --- that is, on every pair of
  neighbouring nodes
- $M$ is symmetric, and it is the identity only for an orthonormal basis,
  which a nodal finite element basis deliberately is not
- lumping replaces it with a diagonal approximation, and switching that on
  is exactly what makes the coupling below disappear

Worth confirming numerically, since everything that follows is a consequence
of $M$ not being the identity.

```{python}
import numpy as np

from pyapprox.pde.galerkin.basis import LagrangeBasis
from pyapprox.pde.galerkin.boundary.implementations import DirichletBC
from pyapprox.pde.galerkin.mesh import StructuredMesh2D
from pyapprox.pde.galerkin.physics import AdvectionDiffusionReaction
from pyapprox.util.backends.numpy import NumpyBkd

bkd = NumpyBkd()

small_mesh = StructuredMesh2D(
    nx=5, ny=5, bounds=[(0.0, 1.0), (0.0, 1.0)], bkd=bkd
)
small_basis = LagrangeBasis(small_mesh, degree=1)
small_physics = AdvectionDiffusionReaction(
    basis=small_basis, diffusivity=1.0, bkd=bkd,
    forcing=lambda x: np.ones(x.shape[1]),
    boundary_conditions=[
        DirichletBC(small_basis, name, 0.0, bkd)
        for name in ("left", "right", "bottom", "top")
    ],
)

mass = np.asarray(bkd.to_numpy(small_physics.mass_matrix()).todense())
print(f"M is {mass.shape[0]}x{mass.shape[1]}, "
      f"symmetric: {np.allclose(mass, mass.T)}")
print(f"identity? {np.allclose(mass, np.eye(mass.shape[0]))}")
print(f"sum of all entries: {mass.sum():.6f}  (the area of the domain)")
```

That last line is a useful check on what $M$ is. The basis functions sum to
one at every point, so $\sum_{ij} M_{ij} = \int_\Omega 1 = |\Omega|$. A
matrix of inner products, not a bookkeeping device.


## The Adjoint Carries $M^{T}$

Discretize @eq-mass-ode in time. Backward Euler gives a residual per step,

$$
\vc{R}_n(\vc{u}_n, \vc{u}_{n-1}, \vc{p})
= M(\vc{u}_n - \vc{u}_{n-1}) - \Delta t\, \vc{F}(\vc{u}_n, t_n, \vc{p})
= \vc{0} ,
$$ {#eq-be-residual}

and the whole trajectory is one large block-bidiagonal system: step $n$
depends on step $n-1$. Its Jacobian has

$$
\frac{\partial \vc{R}_n}{\partial \vc{u}_n}
= M - \Delta t\, \frac{\partial \vc{F}}{\partial \vc{u}} ,
\qquad
\frac{\partial \vc{R}_n}{\partial \vc{u}_{n-1}} = -M .
$$ {#eq-blocks}

Transposing for the adjoint turns the block-bidiagonal system upside down:
the recursion runs **backwards** in time, and $M^{T}$ appears in both
blocks --- in the diagonal one, and as the coupling that carries adjoint
information from step $n$ back to step $n-1$:

$$
\left(M - \Delta t\,
  \frac{\partial \vc{F}}{\partial \vc{u}}\right)^{T} \vc{\lambda}_n
= -\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial \vc{u}_n}\right)
  + M^{T} \vc{\lambda}_{n+1} .
$$ {#eq-adjoint-recursion}

This is the [ODE adjoint recursion](adjoint_ode_concept.qmd) with $M$
inserted, and the constrained rows of
[the steady tutorial](adjoint_steady_pde_concept.qmd) present in **every**
diagonal block rather than once. Neither idea is re-derived here.


## What a Moving Boundary Does

The mass matrix has a consequence that is easy to miss, and it is the
reason $M$ deserves a tutorial rather than a footnote.

Split the degrees of freedom into interior ($i$) and Dirichlet-constrained
($d$), and partition @eq-mass-ode to match:

$$
\begin{bmatrix} M_{ii} & M_{id} \\ M_{di} & M_{dd} \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} \dot{\vc{u}}_i \\ \dot{\vc{u}}_d \end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix} \vc{F}_i \\ \vc{F}_d \end{bmatrix} .
$$ {#eq-partition}

The constrained values are known: $\vc{u}_d = \vc{g}(t)$. Substituting, and
keeping only the interior rows,

$$
M_{ii} \dot{\vc{u}}_i
= \vc{F}_i - M_{id} \dot{\vc{g}} .
$$ {#eq-reduced}

**The interior evolution is forced by the rate of change of the boundary
data**, through $M_{id}$. Not by its value --- by its derivative. If the
boundary condition is constant in time, $\dot{\vc{g}} = \vc{0}$ and the term
vanishes, which is why it is invisible in most examples. As soon as the
boundary moves, it is a real contribution and omitting it is simply wrong.

The block $M_{id}$ is small but not empty: it is nonzero exactly where an
interior basis function overlaps a boundary one.

```{python}
constrained = np.sort(
    bkd.to_numpy(small_physics.constraint_set().dofs()).astype(int)
)
interior = np.array(
    [k for k in range(mass.shape[0]) if k not in set(constrained.tolist())]
)
M_id = mass[np.ix_(interior, constrained)]
couples = (np.abs(M_id) > 1e-14).any(axis=1)

print(f"{len(interior)} interior dofs, {len(constrained)} constrained")
print(f"M_id is {M_id.shape[0]}x{M_id.shape[1]} with "
      f"{int((np.abs(M_id) > 1e-14).sum())} nonzeros")
print(f"{int(couples.sum())} interior dofs feel the boundary's rate")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-mass-coupling
#| fig-cap: "Left: nonzeros of the mass matrix, with constrained degrees of freedom marked on both axes --- $M$ couples every node to its neighbours, constrained or not. Right: the same information on the mesh. The interior nodes drawn in blue are those with a nonzero row in $M_{id}$: they are one layer inward from the boundary, and their evolution feels how fast the boundary data is changing."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from pyapprox_tutorials.figures._galerkin import plot_mass_coupling

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.6))
plot_mass_coupling(
    mass, constrained, bkd.to_numpy(small_basis.dof_coordinates()), axes
)
plt.tight_layout()
```

The coupling reaches exactly one layer of nodes inward. That is the support
of the boundary basis functions, and nothing more.


### Which Steppers Need $\dot{\vc{g}}$ Analytically

One-step implicit methods never see @eq-reduced. Backward Euler steps
@eq-be-residual, which contains $M(\vc{u}_n - \vc{u}_{n-1})$ --- and with
$\vc{u}_d$ pinned to $\vc{g}$ at each end, that difference already supplies
$M_{id}(\vc{g}_n - \vc{g}_{n-1})$, the discrete stand-in for
$\Delta t\, M_{id}\dot{\vc{g}}$. Nothing extra is required of the user.

Stage-based methods evaluate at intermediate times where no such difference
is available, so they need $\dot{\vc{g}}$ **analytically**. Of the steppers
PyApprox registers, `"heun"` is the one that reports itself multistage;
`"forward_euler"`, `"backward_euler"`, `"crank_nicolson"` and
`"implicit_midpoint"` all step from one solution to the next and so supply
the term from their own difference.

PyApprox takes it as an explicit constructor argument rather than
approximating it silently:

``` python
DirichletBC(
    basis, "left", ramp, bkd, value_time_derivative_func=ramp_dot
)
```

Combine `"heun"` with a consistent mass matrix and a time-varying boundary
that lacks `value_time_derivative_func`, and the construction raises rather
than integrating the wrong problem --- naming the three ways out: supply the
analytic derivative, lump the mass, or use a one-step method.


## A Transient Gradient End to End

The problem is the one from
[the steady tutorial](adjoint_steady_pde_concept.qmd) --- a contaminant
released into an obstructed channel, uncertain diffusivity field, one
downstream sensor --- now evolving from a clean initial condition rather
than sitting at steady state.

```{python}
from pyapprox.pde.constitutive.coefficient_functions import (
    NodalFieldDiffusion,
)
from pyapprox.pde.field_maps.kle_factory import (
    create_lognormal_kle_field_map,
)
from pyapprox.pde.parameterizations.galerkin_advection_diffusion import (
    AdvectionDiffusionParameterization,
)
from pyapprox.pde.zoo.obstructed_flow import (
    build_obstructed_mesh,
    extract_velocity_callable,
    solve_obstructed_stokes,
)

NUM_KLE_TERMS = 3
MEAN_DIFFUSIVITY = 0.02

mesh = build_obstructed_mesh(bkd, nrefine=3)
basis = LagrangeBasis(mesh, degree=1)

stokes_mesh = build_obstructed_mesh(bkd, nrefine=2)
stokes_sol, stokes, stokes_vel, stokes_pres = solve_obstructed_stokes(
    stokes_mesh, bkd, reynolds_num=20.0, vel_shape_params=[2.5, 2.5],
    navier_stokes=False,
)
velocity = extract_velocity_callable(
    stokes_sol, stokes, stokes_vel, stokes_pres, basis, bkd,
)


def release(coords):
    """A Gaussian source near the inlet."""
    x, y = coords[0], coords[1]
    return np.exp(-((x - 0.15) ** 2 + (y - 0.5) ** 2) / 0.01)


physics = AdvectionDiffusionReaction(
    basis=basis, diffusivity=NodalFieldDiffusion(basis), bkd=bkd,
    velocity=velocity, forcing=release,
    boundary_conditions=[
        DirichletBC(basis, name, 0.0, bkd)
        for name in mesh.boundary_names()
    ],
)

kle_map = create_lognormal_kle_field_map(
    mesh_coords=basis.dof_coordinates(),
    mean_log_field=bkd.full((basis.ndofs(),), np.log(MEAN_DIFFUSIVITY)),
    bkd=bkd, correlation_length=0.25, num_kle_terms=NUM_KLE_TERMS,
    sigma=0.5,
)
parameterization = AdvectionDiffusionParameterization(
    physics, diffusivity_map=kle_map, bkd=bkd,
)

coords = bkd.to_numpy(basis.dof_coordinates())
constrained_set = set(
    int(d) for d in bkd.to_numpy(physics.constraint_set().dofs())
)
sensor = min(
    (i for i in range(physics.nstates()) if i not in constrained_set),
    key=lambda i: np.hypot(coords[0, i] - 0.85, coords[1, i] - 0.30),
)
print(f"{physics.nstates()} degrees of freedom, sensor at dof {sensor}")
```

The quantity of interest is the concentration at that sensor **at the final
time**. `WeightedEndpointFunctional` expresses that as $Q = \vc{c}^{T}
\vc{u}(T)$ with $\vc{c}$ a unit vector. (Quantities integrated *over* time
are a separate topic, covered in
[transient functionals](transient_functionals_concept.qmd).)

```{python}
from pyapprox.ode.config import TimeIntegrationConfig
from pyapprox.ode.functionals.weighted_endpoint import (
    WeightedEndpointFunctional,
)
from pyapprox.pde.models.galerkin.transient import (
    GalerkinTransientForwardModel,
)

FINAL_TIME = 3.0

weights = bkd.copy(bkd.zeros((physics.nstates(), 1)))
weights[sensor] = 1.0
functional = WeightedEndpointFunctional(weights, NUM_KLE_TERMS, bkd)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
param = bkd.reshape(
    bkd.asarray(rng.normal(size=NUM_KLE_TERMS)), (NUM_KLE_TERMS, 1)
)


def build_model(method, deltat):
    """A transient forward model with its adjoint gradient attached."""
    config = TimeIntegrationConfig(
        method=method, init_time=0.0, final_time=FINAL_TIME, deltat=deltat,
        newton_tol=1e-12, newton_maxiter=20, lumped_mass=False, verbosity=0,
    )
    return GalerkinTransientForwardModel(
        physics, parameterization, bkd.zeros((physics.nstates(),)),
        config, bkd, functional=functional,
    )


model = build_model("backward_euler", 0.05)
print(f"Q = {float(bkd.to_numpy(model(param))[0, 0]):.6e}")
print(f"grad Q = {bkd.to_numpy(model.derivatives().jacobian(param)).ravel()}")
```

`lumped_mass=False` is the choice that matters here: it keeps the
**consistent** mass matrix. Setting it `True` replaces $M$ with a diagonal
approximation, which is cheaper and destroys the $M_{id}$ coupling this
tutorial is about --- a lumped $M$ has no off-diagonal entries, so
@eq-reduced loses its forcing term entirely.

The model satisfies `FunctionProtocol` and carries its derivatives in a
bundle, so it verifies exactly like the steady one --- the checker cannot
tell that a whole trajectory is being solved and unwound inside.

```{python}
from pyapprox.interface.functions.derivative_checks.derivative_checker import (
    DerivativeChecker,
)

fd_eps = bkd.flip(bkd.logspace(-13, -1, 13))
checker = DerivativeChecker(model)
errors = checker.check_derivatives(param, fd_eps=fd_eps)

for name, curve in zip(("gradient", "Hessian-vector product"), errors):
    print(f"{name:<24} best relative error "
          f"{bkd.to_float(bkd.min(curve)):.2e}")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-transient-v-curve
#| fig-cap: "Relative error against finite-difference step size for the transient gradient and Hessian-vector product. The same V as the steady case, with a shallower floor: each difference quotient now stacks the round-off of an entire trajectory of Newton solves rather than of one."
from pyapprox.interface.functions.derivative_checks.plots import (
    plot_fd_error_sweep,
)
from pyapprox_tutorials.figures._style import COLORS

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.5))
plot_fd_error_sweep(
    fd_eps, errors, bkd, ax,
    labels=["gradient", "Hessian-vector product"],
    slope_guides=[1],
)
for line, color in zip(ax.lines, (COLORS["primary"], COLORS["secondary"])):
    line.set_color(color)
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```


## Watching Both Sweeps

The recursion of @eq-adjoint-recursion runs backwards, and it cannot start
until the forward trajectory exists --- every diagonal block needs
$\partial \vc{F}/\partial \vc{u}$ evaluated at $\vc{u}_n$. Both trajectories
are available after the gradient call: the forward one from the model, the
adjoint one from the storage the operator keeps.

```{python}
solutions, solution_times = model.forward_solve(param)
operator = model.hvp_operator(functional)
operator.jacobian(bkd.zeros((physics.nstates(),)), param)
adjoints = operator.storage().get_adjoint_trajectory()

print(f"forward  {bkd.to_numpy(solutions).shape}")
print(f"adjoint  {bkd.to_numpy(adjoints).shape}")
```

Two fields of the same size, and that is the memory cost of the method: the
whole forward trajectory has to be kept, because the backward sweep
linearizes about it.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-sweeps
#| output: asis
from pyapprox_tutorials.figures._galerkin import forward_adjoint_animation

video = forward_adjoint_animation(
    basis, solutions, adjoints, solution_times,
    "adjoint_transient_sweeps.mp4", bkd,
    (coords[0, sensor], coords[1, sensor]), fps=12, stride=2,
)
print(f'<video autoplay loop muted playsinline '
      f'style="width:100%;max-width:960px">'
      f'<source src="{video}" type="video/mp4"></video>')
```

The forward sweep runs first, with the adjoint panel dark because there is
nothing to compute yet. Once the trajectory is complete the clock reverses
and the adjoint sweeps back, with the forward field held at its final state.
Both panels are on a log scale: the forward peak saturates within the first
few frames, so on a linear scale the faint leading edge --- the part that
actually reaches the sensor --- is invisible.

Played this way the two halves of the method are hard to confuse. The plume
spreads outwards from the release, downstream with the flow. The adjoint
spreads outwards from the sensor, **upstream against it**.

It also decays as the sweep proceeds, by three orders of magnitude:

```{python}
adjoint_np = np.abs(bkd.to_numpy(adjoints))
for index in (-1, -11, -21, 0):
    print(f"t = {bkd.to_numpy(solution_times)[index]:4.2f}   "
          f"max |lambda| = {adjoint_np[:, index].max():9.3f}")
```

The adjoint is largest at $t = T$, where it is seeded, and smallest at
$t = 0$. That ordering says something physical: a perturbation applied at
the final instant lands on the sensor immediately and undiluted, while the
same perturbation applied at $t = 0$ has the whole trajectory to diffuse
through before the reading is taken. Early times influence the quantity of
interest, but weakly --- which is exactly the sensitivity the gradient is
made of.


## The Gradient Converges at the Scheme's Order

Here is the question this section settles. The time stepper introduces an
error of its own, on top of the spatial discretization. Backward Euler is
first order in $\Delta t$, Crank--Nicolson second. That is a statement about
$Q$. **Does the gradient inherit it, or lose an order?**

Losing an order would be a reasonable guess --- differentiating usually
costs accuracy. Measure it instead.

```{python}
DELTATS = [0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.025]
REFERENCE_DELTAT = 0.003125

errors_by_case = {}
rates = {}
for method, label in (("backward_euler", "backward Euler"),
                      ("crank_nicolson", "Crank-Nicolson")):
    reference = build_model(method, REFERENCE_DELTAT)
    q_ref = float(bkd.to_numpy(reference(param))[0, 0])
    g_ref = bkd.to_numpy(reference.derivatives().jacobian(param)).ravel()

    q_errors, g_errors = [], []
    for deltat in DELTATS:
        coarse = build_model(method, deltat)
        q = float(bkd.to_numpy(coarse(param))[0, 0])
        g = bkd.to_numpy(coarse.derivatives().jacobian(param)).ravel()
        q_errors.append(abs(q - q_ref) / abs(q_ref))
        g_errors.append(
            np.linalg.norm(g - g_ref) / np.linalg.norm(g_ref)
        )

    errors_by_case[(label, "$Q$")] = q_errors
    errors_by_case[(label, r"$\nabla Q$")] = g_errors
    rates[label] = (
        np.log2(np.array(q_errors[:-1]) / np.array(q_errors[1:])),
        np.log2(np.array(g_errors[:-1]) / np.array(g_errors[1:])),
    )

for label, (q_rate, g_rate) in rates.items():
    print(f"{label:16s} Q rates {np.round(q_rate, 2)}   "
          f"grad Q rates {np.round(g_rate, 2)}")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-temporal-convergence
#| fig-cap: "Temporal convergence of the quantity of interest (circles) and of its gradient (squares), for both schemes, against a finely-stepped reference. Both quantities follow the scheme's own order: slope one for backward Euler, slope two for Crank--Nicolson. The gradient does not lag the value it differentiates."
from pyapprox_tutorials.figures._galerkin import plot_temporal_convergence

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.8))
plot_temporal_convergence(DELTATS, errors_by_case, ax)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The gradient converges at the same order as the quantity it differentiates.

The reason is worth stating, because it is the practical argument for the
**discrete** adjoint over the continuous one. PyApprox differentiates the
discrete time-stepping equations --- @eq-be-residual and its transpose ---
not the underlying PDE. The result is the exact gradient *of the scheme you
actually ran*, whatever $\Delta t$ it used. Its error relative to the true
PDE gradient is inherited entirely from the scheme's own $O(\Delta t^k)$
error, so the two converge together.

The alternative --- discretizing the continuous adjoint PDE separately ---
gives a gradient that is only approximately the derivative of the computed
$Q$. Optimizers notice the difference: a gradient that is not quite the
derivative of the objective it is paired with will stall a line search that
a consistent one walks straight through.

So the choice of $\Delta t$ is a single accuracy knob for both quantities.
Crank--Nicolson at $\Delta t = 0.05$ here delivers a gradient about two
hundred times more accurate than backward Euler at the same step, for one
extra assembly per step.


## Key Takeaways

- A finite element evolution is $M\dot{\vc{u}} = \vc{F}$. The mass matrix
  collects basis-function overlaps, is symmetric and non-diagonal, and sums
  to the area of the domain.
- The transient adjoint is the ODE recursion with $M^{T}$ in both the
  diagonal and the coupling block, run backwards, with constrained rows in
  every block.
- Partitioning $M$ shows the interior evolution is forced by
  $M_{id}\dot{\vc{g}}$ --- the boundary's **rate of change**, reaching one
  layer of nodes inward. One-step implicit methods supply it from their own
  differences; stage-based methods require it analytically, and PyApprox
  enforces that through a protocol rather than trusting the caller.
- $Q$ and $\nabla Q$ converge at the scheme's order, because the discrete
  adjoint differentiates the scheme rather than the PDE.
